**Affect in Deep Knowledge Tracing**

## An ASSISTments Experiment: Methods, Results, and Critical Appraisal

## Completed Colab experiment: 16 October 2026 | Primary dataset: ASSISTments 2012

# **Abstract**

This study examined whether supplied affect-detector scores add consistent, practically relevant predictive information to a recurrent knowledge-tracing model. Two deep knowledge tracing (DKT) models shared the same architecture, student partitions, interaction histories, and tuning budget. The affect model additionally received four standardized scores from the previous completed interaction. The 2012 cohort contained 2,172,029 retained responses from 28,998 students. Five student splits and three training seeds produced 15 paired test comparisons; a separate 2009 baseline benchmark contained no affect model. Future correctness was the endpoint and served only as indirect evidence about knowledge.

On the primary split and training seed, test log loss was 0.531145 without affect and 0.531231 with affect. The baseline-minus-affect difference was −0.000086, with a conditional 95% student-bootstrap interval of \[−0.000290, 0.000118\]. Affect improved aggregate loss in 3 of 15 comparisons, and no comparison reached the configured 1% relative-improvement criterion. Exploratory skill analyses showed heterogeneous effects. On exactly matched primary test responses, the DKT baseline had 5.50% lower log loss than the earlier BKT baseline, although the implementations differed in accessible history and model structure. The results provide little support for a consistent practical benefit from this affect implementation; they do not measure mastery directly or establish that affect is irrelevant to learning.

# **1\. Research Question and Interpretation**

The motivating question was: “Can affect be used as a consistent, relevant factor in predicting mastery of a topic in a knowledge-tracing algorithm?” Because neither dataset supplied an independently validated mastery outcome for this experiment, the operational question was narrower: does previously available predicted affect improve prediction of correctness on a student’s next retained response? “Relevant” was assessed through effect size and a configured practical threshold; “consistent” was examined across splits, training seeds, and skills. None of these checks validates a latent mastery construct.

DKT uses recurrent neural networks to model response sequences, following the general approach introduced by Piech et al. (2015). The present implementation is a documented variant with learned interaction embeddings, a single LSTM layer, and a lagged-affect extension; it is not a reproduction of the original paper’s exact protocol. The earlier BKT experiment provides a descriptive comparison, while the central controlled contrast here is DKT with versus without affect. \[R1, E1–E3\]

# **2\. Data, Reconstruction, and Partitioning**

## **2.1 Retained Cohorts**

**Table 1\. Source size and retained cohorts.**

| Quantity | ASSISTments 2012 | ASSISTments 2009 |
| :---- | :---: | :---: |
| Source CSV rows | 6,123,270 | 401,756 |
| Unique events before filtering | 6,123,270 | 346,860 |
| Retained events | 2,172,029 | 214,417 |
| Retained students | 28,998 | 4,003 |
| Retained skill IDs | 263 | 101 |
| Affect comparison | With and without affect | Baseline only |

Source: archived data\_audit.json records. Counts describe the supplied files and the implemented filters, not the complete historical ASSISTments populations. \[E1\]

An event was identified by student and event ID. The ingestion code reconstructed repeated annotations, rejected conflicting or multiple-skill annotations, required valid identity, skill, outcome, and ordering fields, and retained original problems with a nonempty problem type that did not contain open\_response. Scaffolding records were excluded. In 2012, events were sorted by student, start time, and event ID; a problem beginning before the previously retained problem had ended was removed. In 2009, order\_id supplied chronology. CSV row order was not treated as a timestamp.

The binary outcome was y \= 1 only when the recorded correctness score equaled 1\. For 2012, scores within \[0, 1\] were admissible and values below 1 were coded as unsuccessful; for 2009, only scores already equal to 0 or 1 were admissible. Thus the endpoint is full correctness on the retained problem record. The code does not require attempt\_count \= 1, and the report does not treat a retained event as an independently verified single-attempt mastery test.

The 2012 audit recorded 3,411,457 rows without a skill ID, 303,533 scaffolding events, and 450,500 events overlapping the previous retained problem. These categories come from different filtering stages and can overlap; subtracting them as mutually exclusive losses would be incorrect. Missing or invalid values were not recorded for the four supplied affect columns in the 2012 source audit. The substantial exclusions narrow the population to which the findings apply. The 2009 CSV lacks all four affect columns, so that dataset serves only as a baseline benchmark.

## **2.2 Student-Disjoint Evaluation**

For each split seed, sorted student IDs were shuffled and assigned approximately 70% to training, 15% to validation, and the remainder to test. All retained events from a student stayed in one partition. The five split seeds were 42, 7, 21, 84, and 123\. Split 42 and training seed 101 formed the configured primary comparison. Other splits reuse many students; they assess within-cohort sensitivity rather than provide independent replications.

**Table 2\. Primary partition sizes.**

| Dataset | Partition | Responses | Students |
| :---- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 2012 | Training | 1,507,557 | 20,298 |
| 2012 | Validation | 329,965 | 4,349 |
| 2012 | Test | 334,507 | 4,351 |
| 2009 | Training | 152,861 | 2,802 |
| 2009 | Validation | 31,982 | 600 |
| 2009 | Test | 29,574 | 601 |

Source: report.json, primary student split 42\. Additional 2012 partition sizes are recorded in the archive. \[E1\]

Training determined all weights, feature transformations, and skill support. Validation determined optimizer settings and the selected checkpoint. Test outcomes were used only after model selection. During sequential test prediction, the model could observe the earlier completed responses of the held-out student, but its weights were never updated on test data. This evaluates prediction for new students with accumulating observed histories, not prediction of an entire unseen sequence without feedback.

# **3\. Methodology: The Exact Experimental Contrast**

## **3.1 Chronological Inputs and Causal Alignment**

The shared ingestion routine originally prepares student–skill sequences for BKT. DKT explicitly re-sorts those events into each student’s complete chronological history across skills. At target event t, the current skill k\[t\] selects an output, while the recurrent input contains the previous completed event’s skill and correctness. In the affect model, that same previous event also supplies the four affect scores. These are the previous interaction’s scores, which need not come from the same skill as the target.

![Figure 1. Prediction timing in the implemented DKT models. The current skill selects the output; the recurrent input contains only completed-event information. Lagging prevents same-response leakage within this pipeline, but does not verify the upstream affect detectors’ feature timing or training data.][image1]

Figure 1\. Prediction timing in the implemented DKT models. The current skill selects the output; the recurrent input contains only completed-event information. Lagging prevents same-response leakage within this pipeline, but does not verify the upstream affect detectors’ feature timing or training data.

**Listing 1\. Shift completed-event information before prediction.**

*kt/dkt.py, lines 76–81; excerpt from the archived source.*

completed \= 1 \+ 2 \* targets \+ responses  
tokens \= np.roll(completed, 1\)  
tokens\[first\] \= 0  \# BOS, also used only for masked padding.  
raw\_affect \= transform.transform(frame).astype(np.float32)  
affect \= np.roll(raw\_affect, 1, axis=0)  
affect\[first\] \= 0

targets contains the mapped skill IDs for the chronological rows, and responses contains their binary outcomes. Rolling each completed input by one row makes event t−1 available at event t. Resetting every student’s first row to zero prevents the last event of another student from entering the new history. Zero denotes the beginning-of-sequence token, not an incorrect response. Every retained target, including the first response and chunk boundaries, is scored once.

For example, after a student completes a fractions problem, its response and affect scores can influence the next prediction on decimals. Affect measured on that decimals interaction cannot influence its own prediction. A student’s first prediction instead uses the queried skill, a zero input, and a zero initial state. Although first-response inputs are identical between models, fitted first-response probabilities can differ because the two training procedures learn different global parameters.

## **3.2 Training-Only Preprocessing and Skill Mapping**

The affect variables were frustration, confusion, concentration, and boredom, supplied as four continuous detector-confidence columns. For each split, each score was centered by its training mean and divided by its training standard deviation. Missing values were replaced by the training mean, making their standardized value zero; standardized values were clipped to \[−5, 5\]. A near-zero standard deviation was replaced by 1\. No log transform was applied to these affect variables. Validation and test used the saved training transformation. No behavioral controls such as hints, attempts, or response time entered either DKT model.

**Listing 2\. Apply the fitted affect transformation.**

*kt/data.py, lines 290–293; excerpt from the archived source.*

def transform(self, frame):  
    x \= self.raw(frame)  
    x \= np.where(np.isnan(x), self.mean, x)  
    return np.clip((x \- self.mean) / self.scale, \-5, 5\)

self.mean and self.scale are estimated on the training partition before this method is applied to any partition. The scores describe model-estimated affect; they are not direct observations of a student’s emotional state, and a standardized zero should not be interpreted as psychological neutrality.

A skill received its own ID only if it had at least 50 training responses from at least five training students. Unsupported and unseen skills shared pooled ID 0\. The primary 2012 split had 220 supported skill IDs plus this pooled category. Of its 334,507 test responses, 222 used the pooled category. The token for a completed event was 1 \+ 2 × skill\_ID \+ correctness, reserving token 0 for the beginning of a sequence and masked padding.

## **3.3 Shared DKT Network and the Affect Extension**

Both models used a 32-dimensional learned interaction embedding, one unidirectional LSTM layer with 64 hidden units, and a skill-specific linear output. Dropout with probability 0.1 was applied to the recurrent outputs during training and disabled during evaluation. Only the queried skill’s logit was computed, avoiding a dense output over every skill at every position. This computation is algebraically the same as forming the full linear readout and then selecting the current skill.

Baseline input: u\[t\] \= Embedding(previous skill, previous correctness)

Affect input: u\[t\] \= Embedding(previous skill, previous correctness) \+ Wₐ z\[t−1\]

(h\[t\], c\[t\]) \= LSTM(u\[t\], h\[t−1\], c\[t−1\]);   p\[t\] \= sigmoid(w\[k\] · h\[t\] \+ b\[k\])

Here z\[t−1\] is the four-element standardized affect vector; Wₐ is a learned 32 × 4 projection with no bias. The LSTM hidden state h and cell state c summarize earlier interactions. During training, the readout uses the dropout-transformed hidden output. The prediction p\[t\] is a probability of a correct response on the queried skill, not a calibrated probability that the skill has been mastered.

**Listing 3\. Add affect to the recurrent input.**

*kt/dkt.py, lines 134–136; excerpt from the archived source.*

if use\_affect:  
    \# Identical shared initialization and initial predictions in a pair.  
    nn.init.zeros\_(self.affect\_projection.weight)

*kt/dkt.py, lines 139–143; excerpt from the archived source.*

embedded \= self.embedding(tokens)  
if self.affect\_projection is not None:  
    embedded \= embedded \+ self.affect\_projection(affect)  
hidden, state \= self.lstm(embedded, state)  
hidden \= self.dropout(hidden)

The projection exists only in the affect model. It adds 128 parameters, giving 53,757 parameters versus 53,629 in the primary baseline. It starts at zero, and shared core parameters and random schedules start identically within each candidate/seed pair. Consequently the initial predictions match. After training begins, all parameters can diverge. The extension can change later predictions on any skill through the recurrent state; it is not a single interpretable affect coefficient or a direct learning-rate adjustment as in the earlier BKT extension.

## **3.4 Stateful Training and Optimization**

Students were grouped into batches of at most 64 with similar sequence lengths to reduce padding. Whole batches were shuffled each epoch while within-student chronology was preserved. Histories were processed in chunks of up to 128 events. Hidden and cell states continued across chunks, but gradients were detached at each chunk boundary: this is truncated backpropagation through time. Forward prediction therefore retains earlier history even though a gradient cannot propagate without limit through that history. Padding never contributes to loss, and recurrent states never pass between students.

Binary cross-entropy was optimized with AdamW and weight decay 0.0001. Rather than give each small tail chunk a separate adaptive-optimizer update, gradients accumulated until at least 64 × 128 \= 8,192 valid events were available. They were normalized by the actual accumulated count, clipped to a global norm of 5, and then applied. The final remainder of an epoch could be smaller. This reduces disproportionate updates from tiny tails; it does not guarantee equal influence under an adaptive optimizer. Floating-point training used float32.

**Listing 4\. Accumulate valid events before updating the model.**

*kt/dkt.py, lines 207–211; excerpt from the archived source.*

accumulated \+= count  
if accumulated \>= denominator:  
    grad\_max \= torch.maximum(grad\_max, step(accumulated))  
    steps \+= 1  
    accumulated \= 0

The step helper rescales the accumulated gradients by the nominal budget divided by the actual event count, clips their norm, and calls AdamW. State detachment occurs before each chunk’s forward pass. This excerpt omits the separate final-remainder update; the full source retains it.

## **3.5 Validation Selection and Repeated Training Seeds**

The common candidate grid contained learning rates 0.0003, 0.001, and 0.003; architecture, dropout, and weight decay stayed fixed. Each model was tuned separately on the first training seed, 101, using minimum validation log loss. Training seeds 202 and 303 then repeated the selected settings rather than retuning the grid or choosing the best initialization. Each repeated fit still used validation to select its own checkpoint. All three training seeds were reported.

Each candidate allowed at most 25 epochs and at least five epochs. Early stopping used patience four and a minimum meaningful validation improvement of 0.00001. The checkpoint rule retained every strictly lower validation loss, even when the decrease was too small to reset the patience counter. Thus the selected checkpoint and stopping counter have related but distinct definitions. Ties in candidate validation loss select the first grid entry.

**Listing 5\. Separate best-checkpoint tracking from the patience counter.**

*kt/dkt\_experiment.py, lines 160–162; excerpt from the archived source.*

if val\_loss \< best:  
    best \= val\_loss  
    best\_epoch \= epoch

*kt/dkt\_experiment.py, lines 166–169; excerpt from the archived source.*

if val\_loss \< stopping\_best \- config.min\_delta:  
    stopping\_best, stale \= val\_loss, 0  
else:  
    stale \+= 1

The checkpoint is saved immediately after best\_epoch is assigned in the full source. The second excerpt updates the stopping counter. Neither branch uses test outcomes. The source excerpts throughout this report preserve code tokens and relative indentation; only shared outer indentation is removed, and separate ranges are identified explicitly. They are explanatory excerpts, not standalone scripts.

The total budget was 50 fits for 2012: five splits × two models × (three tuning candidates plus two repeated fits). The 2009 baseline added five fits, for 55 overall. All selected models used learning rate 0.003. Because selection occurred on a finite grid and under a finite epoch budget, this does not establish global optimality or equal adequacy of every candidate’s optimization.

## **3.6 A Detailed Account of the Affect Pathway**

### **What Enters the Network and What Preprocessing Means**

The network receives four supplied detector scores, not an observed emotional diagnosis or a new classification target. The columns frustrated, confused, concentrating, and bored retain their separate coordinates. No winner-take-all emotion, affect average, or softmax normalization is applied. Their values need not form a four-category probability distribution, and this experiment does not establish their psychological calibration.

The shared FeatureTransform fits each coordinate’s mean and population standard deviation using retained training responses. It then applies mean imputation and clipping to ±5 standardized units, without a logarithmic transform. This is a response-weighted population transform, not a personal emotional baseline for each learner. A zero coordinate represents the training mean, or a mean-imputed missing value; it does not mean that an emotion is absent. No missingness indicator is passed to DKT.

Preprocessing precedes temporal shifting. Despite the local variable name raw\_affect in Listing 1, that array already contains transformed scores. The array is shifted by one completed student interaction, and the first row of every student is reset to zero. Consequently, the score for event t can first enter the prediction for event t+1. The source event may be on a different skill, but it is always an earlier retained event in that student’s chronology.

### **A Four-Dimensional Signal Added to an Interaction Embedding**

Write e\[t\] for the 32-dimensional embedding of the previous skill–correctness token, z\[t−1\] for the four standardized scores, and W\_aff for the learned 32 × 4 projection. The affect model forms u\[t\] \= e\[t\] \+ W\_aff z\[t−1\]. The baseline uses u\[t\] \= e\[t\]. This is addition in a shared 32-dimensional space, rather than concatenation into a 36-dimensional input. The LSTM architecture and its input width are therefore identical between arms.

Each column of W\_aff specifies a direction in embedding space. For a hypothetical z \= \[1, 0, 0, 0\], the added vector is exactly its frustration column; for z \= \[1, 0, 0, −1\], it is the frustration column minus the boredom column. These identities explain the computation without implying that either vector occurs in the data. There is no projection bias, so an all-zero feature vector adds exactly zero at that step.

### **How the Affect Vector Reaches Memory and Prediction**

The equations below expand the nn.LSTM call used in the archived network. Let i, f, and o be the input, forget, and output gates, v a candidate cell update, and c and h the cell and hidden states. A matrices multiply the current input u; B matrices multiply the preceding hidden state. Each b combines the implementation’s input and recurrent biases. σ denotes the sigmoid; \* denotes elementwise multiplication.

i\[t\] \= σ(A\_i u\[t\] \+ B\_i h\[t−1\] \+ b\_i)

f\[t\] \= σ(A\_f u\[t\] \+ B\_f h\[t−1\] \+ b\_f)

v\[t\] \= tanh(A\_v u\[t\] \+ B\_v h\[t−1\] \+ b\_v)

o\[t\] \= σ(A\_o u\[t\] \+ B\_o h\[t−1\] \+ b\_o)

c\[t\] \= f\[t\] \* c\[t−1\] \+ i\[t\] \* v\[t\]

h\[t\] \= o\[t\] \* tanh(c\[t\])

Gate equations follow the [PyTorch 2.11 LSTM reference](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.11/generated/torch.nn.LSTM.html). The external affect projection is defined by this experiment’s kt/dkt.py; it is distinct from PyTorch’s optional internal LSTM output projection.

Substituting u\[t\] \= e\[t\] \+ W\_aff z\[t−1\] shows the direct affect term A\_i W\_aff z\[t−1\] in the input gate, with analogous terms in the other gates and candidate update. Thus affect can change what information is written, retained, or exposed by the memory. The four input coordinates share one projection across skills, but the resulting response need not be the same across histories because the gates also depend on h\[t−1\] and c\[t−1\]. This is an implication of the implemented equations, not an observed decomposition of fitted effects.

The queried current skill selects a linear output: p\[t\] \= sigmoid(w\[k\] · h\[t\] \+ b\[k\]) at evaluation. It does not enter the current recurrent input as a separate current-skill embedding. After the current response is observed, that skill and correctness become part of the next step’s token. Because each queried skill has its own output weights, the same affect-altered hidden state may increase one skill’s predicted correctness and decrease another’s.

There is therefore no single DKT coefficient with the interpretation “one standard deviation more frustration changes learning odds by this factor.” Projection entries are intermediate representation weights, not direct effects on correctness or mastery. Their magnitudes or signs alone cannot establish feature importance, emotional mechanisms, or comparability with BKT’s four transition coefficients.

### **Learning an Affect Pathway From Response Errors**

The affect extension is trained through the same response binary cross-entropy as the baseline. There is no separate emotional-state loss, affect reconstruction task, or observed mastery target. For a queried logit, the response loss sends an error through the skill readout and recurrent computation to the projection. At one use of the input, the chain rule gives:

∂L / ∂W\_aff \= (∂L / ∂u\[t\]) z\[t−1\]T

The superscript T denotes vector transpose. Contributions accumulate across valid steps and students, including later losses whose computational paths reach that input. This equation explains why initializing W\_aff to zero does not freeze it: a nonzero feature vector and a nonzero upstream gradient can update the projection even when its current output is zero. Initializing the projection at zero instead makes paired models begin with the same shared predictions.

Once updates begin, embeddings, recurrent weights, output weights, and the projection are all trainable. The two models can consequently diverge throughout the network. AdamW weight decay applies to the trained parameters, and dropout is applied after the LSTM output during training. The code does not randomly drop individual affect coordinates as a dedicated affect-ablation procedure. Evaluation disables dropout but retains the learned affect pathway.

### **Forward Memory and Gradient History Are Different**

Affect can persist through hidden and cell states beyond the immediately following interaction. With events A1, B1, and A2, A1’s affect enters at B1; B1’s affect enters at A2; A1 may still influence A2 through carried memory. This permits cross-skill dependence but does not identify a psychological transfer mechanism. At a new student, both state and the lagged input reset, preventing information transfer between students.

The 128-event chunk boundary detaches gradients while carrying the numerical state forward. A later prediction may therefore depend on earlier affect that is represented in that state, even though its loss cannot backpropagate through computations before the boundary. The lagged feature for the first event of a new chunk is still available because shifting is performed over the complete student sequence before chunking. Padding is masked from loss, and the last event’s affect has no later retained target in which to be consumed.

These details limit interpretation of a small aggregate effect. It could reflect a weak incremental signal, redundant response-history information, an unsuitable lag or representation, or incomplete learning under the finite training procedure. The experiment does not distinguish those explanations. Zeroing one current vector, zeroing a full history, and retraining without affect answer different questions; none directly estimates the causal effect of emotion on learning.

Implementation basis: archived kt/dkt.py (Sequences.build, DKT.forward, \_carry, and train\_epoch), kt/data.py (FeatureTransform), and kt/dkt\_experiment.py (model construction and selection). Gate and gradient explanations describe the executed architecture; no new model or ablation was fitted.

# **4\. Evaluation and Uncertainty**

The primary endpoint was mean binary log loss over retained test responses, using natural logarithms. A student with more retained responses therefore contributes more to this estimand. The implementation computes each response’s loss stably from its logit and saves that value, avoiding distortions when a sigmoid probability rounds to 0 or 1\. Secondary metrics were ROC AUC, Brier score, accuracy at a fixed probability threshold of 0.5, and expected calibration error (ECE) over ten fixed-width probability bins.

Δ \= mean loss without affect − mean loss with affect

Relative improvement (%) \= 100 × Δ / mean loss without affect

Positive Δ favors affect. The configured practical criterion was a relative reduction of at least 1%; on the primary baseline, this corresponds to an absolute reduction of approximately 0.005311. This was a local decision rule recorded in the run configuration, not an externally registered threshold or a measured educational utility. There was no formal equivalence test or prospective power calculation. Failure to reach the criterion is not proof of an exactly zero effect.

Each pair used 2,000 bootstrap samples of whole held-out students. For each sampled student, all paired response-loss contributions remained together; losses were re-aggregated by the total number of sampled responses. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles formed a 95% interval. These intervals are conditional on the particular trained models and split. They omit uncertainty from retraining, hyperparameter selection, and sampling new schools. Training-seed variation was examined separately, with no pooled significance claim or ensemble.

Additional topic analyses in this report are exploratory. A review-stage support rule required at least 100 test responses from at least 20 test students per skill within a split; this is separate from the training support rule and was not a preregistered analysis. Skill-level directions and sign counts are descriptive, not multiplicity-adjusted tests. The 15 comparisons overlap in students, skills, and training data, so they must not be interpreted as 15 independent experiments. \[E2\]

# **5\. Results**

## **5.1 Primary Comparison**

**Table 3\. Primary held-out performance (split 42, training seed 101).**

| Metric | Without affect | With affect |
| :---- | :---: | :---: |
| Log loss ↓ | 0.531145 | 0.531231 |
| ROC AUC ↑ | 0.731653 | 0.731517 |
| Brier score ↓ | 0.176843 | 0.176872 |
| Accuracy ↑ | 0.741940 | 0.741700 |
| Ten-bin ECE ↓ | 0.001563 | 0.001526 |
| Test responses | 334,507 | 334,507 |

Arrows indicate the favorable direction. Both models were scored on identical ordered events and outcomes. Source: archived test predictions and independently reproduced metrics. \[E1, E2\]

The primary affect model had slightly higher log loss: Δ \= −0.00008615, or a relative change of −0.01622% under the improvement convention. Its 95% interval was \[−0.00029040, 0.00011787\]. Brier and accuracy differences also had intervals spanning zero. The affect model’s marginally lower ECE does not overturn this result: ECE is a bin-dependent secondary diagnostic and was not the selection or primary evaluation criterion.

## **5.2 Variation Across Splits and Initializations**

The configured 1% practical threshold is approximately 5.3 on this scale and lies beyond the displayed range. Intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons and should not be pooled across overlapping splits.][image2]

Affect reduced aggregate test loss in 3 of 15 comparisons and increased it in 12\. Fourteen intervals included zero. The exception was split 123, training seed 303: Δ \= 0.00068613, interval \[0.00030156, 0.00107508\], and relative improvement 0.12899%. This was the largest observed gain, but it remained well below 1%. It arose in a secondary comparison and was not stable across the other training seeds for that split. Selecting it alone would misrepresent the experiment.

**Table 4\. Descriptive variation across three training seeds within each split.**

| Split seed | Mean Δ | SD of Δ | Seeds favoring affect |
| :---- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 42 | \-0.000010 | 0.000146 | 1 |
| 7 | \-0.000105 | 0.000059 | 0 |
| 21 | \-0.000126 | 0.000100 | 0 |
| 84 | \-0.000089 | 0.000066 | 0 |
| 123 | 0.000160 | 0.000503 | 2 |

Each mean and sample SD describes three fitted-model differences. These are not estimates from independent study replications, and no pooled confidence interval is asserted. \[E2\]

No comparison met the configured practical criterion. The varying signs, the isolated larger gain, and the overlapping intervals provide little support for a reliable incremental advantage in this model family and cohort. They do not establish that an arbitrarily small effect is absent, nor do they compare every possible way to represent affect.

![Figure 3. Training and validation log-loss trajectories for the two selected primary fits. Both retained epoch 10 and stopped after epoch 14. Training curves reflect the changing model and active dropout within an epoch; validation uses fixed end-of-epoch weights and disabled dropout, so the two curves are related diagnostics rather than strictly comparable measurements.][image3]

Training curves reflect the changing model and active dropout within an epoch; validation uses fixed end-of-epoch weights and disabled dropout, so the two curves are related diagnostics rather than strictly comparable measurements.

All 30 selected 2012 fits satisfied the patience condition. Their selected epochs ranged from 9 to 14, and their completed training lengths ranged from 11 to 18 epochs. Of all 55 candidate fits, 20 exhausted the 25-epoch budget. Nineteen of those were unselected. The one selected fit that exhausted its budget was the 2009 baseline at training seed 101; its best checkpoint was epoch 23\. This warning does not describe an unfinished selected 2012 affect comparison, but the candidate caps still constrain claims about the completeness of the tuning search.

Under the exploratory test-support rule, 72 of 145 primary-split skills had lower affect-model loss. Figure 5\. Distribution of the number of comparisons favoring affect among 137 skill IDs supported in all 15 comparisons. Support required at least 100 test responses and 20 test students per split. Counts reuse students and data; they are exploratory and must not be compared with an independent binomial model. \[E2\]

At the student level, 49.0% of primary test students had lower mean loss under the affect model; across comparisons, the corresponding fraction ranged from 47.0% to 51.5%. These unweighted sign counts describe how often a student’s average loss decreased. They do not replace the response-weighted primary estimand and do not establish which students benefit reliably.

# **6\. Relation to BKT and the 2009 Benchmark**

## **6.1 Matched Primary Responses, Different Model Histories**

**Table 6\. Descriptive primary baseline comparison on 334,507 matched responses.**

| Metric | BKT without affect | DKT without affect |
| :---- | :---: | :---: |
| Log loss | 0.562044 | 0.531145 |
| ROC AUC | 0.681533 | 0.731653 |
| Brier score | 0.189114 | 0.176843 |
| Accuracy | 0.723967 | 0.741940 |

Student, event, and skill identifiers matched one-to-one; outcomes and timestamps were identical. This is a comparison of the implemented pipelines, without an architecture-specific causal interpretation. \[E2, E3\]

The DKT baseline reduced primary test log loss by approximately 5.50% relative to the BKT baseline and improved the other displayed metrics. This is substantially larger than the observed incremental affect effects. However, DKT processes each student’s cross-skill sequence, whereas the earlier BKT maintains separate student–skill states. The models also differ in capacity, parameterization, optimization, and tuning. Their difference therefore cannot be attributed solely to recurrence or neural-network depth. Prior work has likewise shown that conclusions about DKT versus BKT depend on the statistical regularities the comparison models can represent. \[R2\]

The earlier BKT experiment found small positive affect-related loss reductions across its five splits, all below the same 1% practical criterion. The DKT follow-up adds a useful qualification: the direction of the affect increment did not persist reliably across DKT training seeds and splits, even though its baseline predicted correctness more accurately. One possible explanation is that richer response histories already capture some information correlated with the detector scores. This is an interpretation to test, not a mechanism established by the present results.

## **6.2 Separate 2009 Baseline Benchmark**

**Table 7\. DKT baseline performance on the 2009 primary test partition.**

| Training seed | Log loss | ROC AUC | Accuracy |
| :---- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 101 | 0.543354 | 0.748461 | 0.731487 |
| 202 | 0.542027 | 0.751111 | 0.732096 |
| 303 | 0.543974 | 0.747943 | 0.730168 |

All three fits used 29,574 test responses from 601 students. No 2009 affect model was trained. \[E1\]

The 2009 results demonstrate operation on a second supplied dataset, but cannot replicate an affect effect because the relevant columns are absent. The selected seed-101 fit reached its epoch cap before satisfying patience; its checkpoint at epoch 23 remains the minimum-validation-loss model within the allowed budget. Cross-year differences should not be interpreted as temporal generalization: models were fitted separately, and data content and preprocessing constraints differ.

# **7\. Limitations and Implications**

## **7.1 Outcome Validity and Causal Scope**

The principal limitation is the mismatch between the broad mastery question and the observed endpoint. A correct response can depend on item difficulty, guessing, task familiarity, help, and other factors. Neither the recurrent state nor the skill-specific output was validated against an independent mastery assessment. The study supports claims about predictive correctness under this protocol, not a conclusion that mastery was measured or improved. The observational design also cannot show that affect causes learning.

## **7.2 Affect Provenance and Representation**

The four inputs are outputs of pre-existing affect detectors. The archived files do not establish their training populations, validation quality, exact feature windows, or independence from these evaluation students. Shifting a supplied score by one completed interaction prevents its direct same-row use in this implementation, but cannot repair future information or outcome dependence already embedded upstream. Detector confidence may also reflect response behavior correlated with correctness rather than a distinct affect construct.

The model adds 128 parameters and allows their downstream effect to be nonlinear and history-dependent. No shuffled-affect, matched-capacity noise, behavior-control, or individual-affect ablation was trained. Consequently any positive difference would not uniquely establish affect-specific information, and a small difference cannot identify which component failed. The lag and four-score representation are only one plausible design. Projection weights alone are not causal effects or straightforward psychological coefficients.

## **7.3 Generalization, Dependence, and Statistical Limits**

The test students are held out within the same datasets, not from independently sampled schools or a future deployment period. Item and school contexts can overlap across partitions. Repeated splits overlap; training seeds do not create new populations. Bootstrap intervals account for within-student response dependence conditional on fitted models, but do not incorporate school-level clustering, selection uncertainty, or retraining. The single positive secondary interval was not adjusted for the many comparisons. An absence of a primary advantage should be described as limited evidence under this design rather than universal equivalence.

The retained cohort excludes many source rows, multi-skill records, scaffolding, and overlapping problems. Excluding records also removes context from the histories available to both models. Rare and unseen skills share a pooled representation. These choices improve definitional and timing control, but restrict generalization. Response weighting emphasizes students with longer retained histories; the unweighted student sign analysis answers a different question.

## **7.4 Training Budget and Comparison Design**

Architecture was fixed at a 32-dimensional embedding and 64 hidden units. Learning-rate search, 25-epoch limits, and three training seeds are finite, and 20 candidates exhausted the epoch budget. Satisfying early-stopping patience does not prove optimizer convergence or that the architecture is sufficient. Truncating gradients to 128-event chunks restricts what long-range dependencies training can learn, despite preserving forward state. The observed results do not establish the best attainable DKT performance or rule out a better affect extension.

The two DKT models share their design and selection rules, but each is fitted independently. Even zero affect at a particular test event does not force their learned predictions to match. The BKT comparison introduces larger differences in available history and model structure. Its useful descriptive advantage therefore should not be conflated with a clean architecture-only experiment.

# **8\. Reproducibility and Priorities for Further Work**

The uploaded archive contained 656 entries, including all 55 candidate histories and checkpoints, 33 selected test-prediction files, and corresponding validation predictions. Review verified 75 integrity manifests, matched the external HTML to the archived report, and confirmed that 24 saved source/test/dependency files matched the local implementation. All 33 selected test metric sets and all 15 paired log-loss bootstrap intervals were independently reproduced from saved predictions. These checks support internal consistency and reproducibility of the recorded analysis; hashes do not prove the original scientific validity of the data or detectors. \[E2\]

The completed run used a Tesla T4 GPU, Python 3.13.15, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, NumPy 2.1.3, pandas 2.2.3, SciPy 1.16.3, and Numba 0.61.2. The saved logs report 39 passing regression tests and a deterministic device-training check. Recorded suite wall time was 2,687 seconds (44.8 minutes), from suite start through analysis before final report/manifest completion; it excludes notebook installation, final export, and browser download. Peak PyTorch allocated CUDA memory was approximately 181.3 MiB. This is one observed runtime, not a controlled hardware benchmark. Deterministic settings do not guarantee identical results across software versions or devices. \[E1, R3\]

The most informative next experiments would test affect specificity and external validity. A shuffled-affect control and a matched-capacity noise projection would help separate affect information from added parameters. Behavioral-control models and one-score-at-a-time ablations would examine redundancy. A comparison that gives BKT and DKT matched history access would improve architectural interpretation. An independently collected mastery assessment and prospective, documented affect estimates would address the larger research question more directly.

Any expanded tuning, representation changes, or subgroup hypotheses chosen after inspecting these results should be labeled exploratory and evaluated on fresh held-out data for confirmation. More computation alone would not resolve detector provenance, mastery validity, or the dependence of repeated splits. Existing artifacts are sufficient to write the present report; these are proposed extensions, not completed analyses.

# **9\. Conclusion**

Under the implemented DKT protocol, the supplied lagged affect scores did not provide a consistent or practically substantial improvement in future-correctness prediction. The primary effect was slightly unfavorable and uncertain, only three of fifteen paired comparisons favored affect, and all effects fell below the configured practical threshold. Skill and student diagnostics were mixed. The DKT baseline improved substantially over the earlier BKT baseline on matched responses, but that result reflects multiple model and history differences. The experiment therefore narrows the claim to this predictive setup: it offers little support for the incremental utility of this affect representation while leaving the broader role of affect in learning and mastery unresolved.
